### 4.3 The case of a closed strip

Suppose now that all roots $\alpha$ of $P$ satisfy $|\operatorname{Re}\alpha|\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Recall that we have $P(x)=P_{*}(x)Q\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)$ $\times Q\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)$ where all roots of $P_{*}(x)$ satisfy $|\operatorname{Re}x|<\frac{1}{2}$ and all roots of $Q(x)$ belong to ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . For any $R\in\mathbb{C}[x]$ write $R=R_{1}Q+R_{0}$ , where $\deg R_{0}<\deg Q$ .

By Proposition 3.10 each $g_{t}$ -twisted trace can be obtained as

$$ T(R(z))=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}R_{1}(x)Q(x)w(x)|{\rm d}x|+\phi(R_{0}), $$

where $w(x)={\rm e}^{2\pi{\rm i}cx}\frac{G({\rm e}^{2\pi{\rm i}x})}{\mathbf{P}({\rm e}^{2\pi{\rm i}x})}$ and $\phi$ is any linear functional.

#### Proposition 4.14.

Suppose that $T$ is a trace as above and $w(x)$ has poles on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . Then $T$ does not give a positive definite form.

#### Proof.

Let $Q_{*}(x)=Q(x)\overline{Q}(-x)$ ; note that $Q_{*}(x)\geq 0$ for $x\in{\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . Then there exists a linear functional $\psi$ such that for any $R=R_{1}Q_{*}+R_{0}$ with $\deg R_{0}<\deg Q_{*}$ we have

$$ T(R(z))=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}R_{1}(x)Q_{*}(x)w(x)|{\rm d}x|+\psi(R_{0}). $$

Suppose that $T$ gives a positive definite form. Then $T(S(z)\overline{S}(-z))>0$ for all nonzero $S\in\mathbb{C}[x]$ . Taking $S(x)=Q_{*}(x)S_{1}(x)$ and using Lemma 4.2, we deduce that $Q_{*}^{2}(x)w(x)$ , hence $w(x)$ , is nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . In particular, all poles of $w(x)$ have order at least $2$ .

Without loss of generality assume that $w(x)$ has a pole at zero. Let

$$ R_{n}(x):=(F_{n}Q_{*}+b)\big(\overline{F_{n}}Q_{*}+b\big), $$

where $b\in\mathbb{R}$ . Suppose that $F_{n}$ is a sequence of polynomials that tends to the function $f:=\chi_{(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)}$ (the characteristic function of the interval) in the space $L^{2}\big({\rm i}\mathbb{R},(Q_{*}+Q_{*}^{2}\big)w)$ . In particular, $F_{n}$ tends to $f$ in the spaces $L^{2}({\rm i}\mathbb{R},Q_{*}w)$ and $L^{2}\big({\rm i}\mathbb{R},Q_{*}^{2}w\big)$ . Then we deduce from the Cauchy–Schwartz inequality that $F_{n}\overline{F_{n}}$ tends to $f^{2}$ in the space $L^{1}\big({\rm i}\mathbb{R},Q_{*}^{2}w\big)$ , and $F_{n}$ and $\overline{F_{n}}$ tend to $f$ in $L^{1}({\rm i}\mathbb{R},Q_{*}w)$ .

We have

$$ \displaystyle T(R_{n}(z))=T\big(\big(F_{n}\overline{F_{n}}Q_{*}+F_{n}b+\overline{F_{n}}b\big)(z)Q_{*}(z)+b^{2}\big) \displaystyle\hphantom{T(R_n(z))}{}=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}\big(F_{n}\overline{F_{n}}Q_{*}^{2}+F_{n}bQ_{*}+\overline{F_{n}}bQ_{*}\big)w|{\rm d}x|+\phi\big(b^{2}\big). $$

Therefore, when $n$ tends to infinity,

$$ T(R_{n}(z))\to\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}\big(f^{2}Q_{*}^{2}+2fbQ_{*}\big)w|{\rm d}x|+\phi\big(b^{2}\big). $$

We have $\phi\big(b^{2}\big)=Cb^{2}$ for some $C\geq 0$ . Suppose that $w$ has a pole of order $M\geq 2$ at $0$ and $Q_{*}$ has a zero of order $N>0$ at $0$ . Then $Q_{*}w$ has a zero of order $N-M$ at zero and $Q_{*}^{2}w$ has a zero of order $2N-M$ at zero. We deduce that

$$ \int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}F_{n}Q_{*}w|{\rm d}x|\to c_{1}\varepsilon^{N-M+1},\qquad\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}F_{n}Q_{*}^{2}w|{\rm d}x|\to c_{2}\varepsilon^{2N-M+1},\qquad n\to\infty, $$

where $c_{1}=c_{1}(\varepsilon)$ , $c_{2}=c_{2}(\varepsilon)$ are functions having strictly positive limits at $\varepsilon=0$ . Therefore

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}T(R_{n}(z))=Cb^{2}+2c_{1}\varepsilon^{N-M+1}b+c_{2}\varepsilon^{2N-M+1}. $$

This is a quadratic polynomial of $b$ with discriminant

$$ D=4\varepsilon^{2N-2M+2}\big(c_{1}^{2}-Cc_{2}\varepsilon^{M-1}\big). $$

Since $M{\geq}2$ , for small $\varepsilon$ this discriminant is positive. In particular, for some $b$ , $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}T(R_{n}(z)){<}0,$ so for this $b$ and some $n$ , $T(R_{n}(z))<0$ , a contradiction. ∎

Now we are left with the case when $w(x)$ has no poles on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . In this case $T(R(z))=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}R(x)w(x)|{\rm d}x|+\eta(R_{0})$ , where $\eta$ is some linear functional.

#### Proposition 4.15.

$T$ gives a positive definite form only when $\eta(R_{0})=\sum_{j}c_{j}R_{0}(z_{j})$ , where $c_{j}\geq 0$ and $z_{j}\in{\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ are the roots of $Q$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose that this is not the case. Then it is easy to find a polynomial $S$ such that $\eta\big(\big(S\overline{S}\big)_{0}\big)<0$ . Then using Lemma 4.2(2) for $M=Q$ , we find $F_{n}$ such that $F_{n}Q+S$ tends to zero in $L^{2}({\rm i}\mathbb{R},w)$ . We deduce that

$$ T\big((F_{n}Q+S)(z)\overline{(F_{n}Q+S)}(z)\big)\to\eta\big((S\overline{S})_{0}\big)<0, $$

which gives a contradiction. ∎

In the proof of Proposition 4.14 we got that $w$ is nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . We also note that $Q(z)$ divides $P\big(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)$ , hence

$$ T\big(R\big(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\overline{R}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}-z\big)P\big(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\big)=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}R\big(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\overline{R}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}-z\big)P\big(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)w(z)|dz|. $$

Using the proof of Proposition 4.4 we see that $\lambda P(z)w\big(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\big)$ is nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . Assume that $Q\big(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)Q\big(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\big)$ is positive on $\mathbb{R}$ . Then this is equivalent to $\lambda P_{*}(z)w\big(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\big)$ being nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . So we have proved the following theorem.

#### Theorem 4.16.

Suppose that $P(x)=P_{*}(x)Q\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)Q\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)$ , where all roots of $P_{*}$ belong to the set $|\operatorname{Re}x|<\frac{1}{2}$ and all roots of $Q$ belong to ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . Suppose that $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}$ are all the different roots of $Q$ . Then positive traces $T$ are in one-to-one correspondence with $\widetilde{T}$ , $c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}\geq 0$ , where $\widetilde{T}$ is a positive trace for $P_{*}$ ; namely,

$$ T(R(z))=\widetilde{T}(R(z))+\sum c_{i}R(\alpha_{i}). $$

### 4.4 The general case

Let $\mathcal{A}$ is be a filtered quantization of $A$ with conjugation $\rho$ given by formula (2.3). Let $P(x)$ be its parameter. Let $\widetilde{P}(x)$ be the polynomial defined in Section 3.5: it has the same degree as $P(x)$ and its roots are obtained from the roots of $P(x)$ by minimal integer shift into the strip $|\operatorname{Re}x|\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Also recall from Section 3.5 that $P_{\circ}$ denotes the following polynomial: all roots of $P_{\circ}$ belong to strip $|\operatorname{Re}x|\leq\frac{1}{2}$ and the multiplicity of $\alpha,|\operatorname{Re}\alpha|\leq\frac{1}{2}$ in $P_{\circ}$ equals to multiplicity of $\alpha$ in $P$ . Let $n_{\circ}:=\deg(P_{\circ})$ .

Proposition 3.11 says that any trace $T$ can be represented as $T=\Phi+\widetilde{T}$ , where $\Phi$ is a linear functional such that

$$ \Phi(R)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{k}c_{jk}R^{(k)}(z_{j}), $$

$z_{j}\notin{\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ , and $\widetilde{T}$ is a trace for $\widetilde{P}$ . Furthermore, if $\Phi=0$ then $T$ is just a trace for $P_{\circ}$ .

#### Proposition 4.17.

Let $T$ be a trace such that $\Phi\neq 0$ . Then $T$ does not give a positive definite form.

#### Proof.

For big enough $k$ we have $\Phi((x-z_{1})^{k}\cdots(x-z_{m})^{k}\mathbb{C}[x])=0$ . Recall that there exists polynomial $Q_{*}(x)$ nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ such that for $R=R_{1}Q_{*}+R_{0}$ , $\deg R_{0}<\deg Q_{*}$ , we have $\widetilde{T}(R)=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}R_{1}Q_{*}w|{\rm d}x|+\psi(R_{0})$ , where $\psi$ is some linear functional. Let $U(x)$ be a polynomial divisible by $Q_{*}$ such that $\Phi(U(x)\mathbb{C}[x])=0$ .

Let $L$ be any polynomial. Using Lemma 4.2 for $M=U$ , we find a sequence $G_{n}=US_{n}$ that tends to $L$ in the space $L^{2}({\rm i}\mathbb{R},Q_{*}w|{\rm d}x|)$ . We deduce that $H_{n}(x):=(G_{n}(x)-L(x))(\overline{G_{n}}(-x)-\overline{L}(-x))$ tends to zero in $L^{1}({\rm i}\mathbb{R},Q_{*}w)$ . We have $\widetilde{T}(H_{n}(z)Q_{*}(z))=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}H_{n}(x)Q_{*}w|{\rm d}x|$ . We conclude that $\widetilde{T}(H_{n}(z)Q_{*}(z))=\|H_{n}\|_{L^{1}({\rm i}\mathbb{R},Q_{*}w)}$ tends to zero when $n$ tends to infinity.

It follows that $T(H_{n}(z))$ tends to $\Phi(Q_{*}(x)H_{n}(x))=\Phi\big(Q_{*}(x)L(x)\overline{L}(-x)\big)$ . Since $H_{n}$ is nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ , we have $T(H_{n}(z))>0$ . Now we get a contradiction with

#### Lemma 4.18.

There exists $F(x)\in\mathbb{C}[x]$ such that $\Phi\big(Q_{*}(x)F(x)\overline{F}(-x)\big)<0$ .

#### Proof.

Let $r$ be the biggest number such that there exists $j$ with $c_{jr}\neq 0$ . Let

$$ F(x):=G(x)(x-z_{1})^{r+1}\cdots(x-z_{j})^{r}\cdots(x-z_{m})^{r+1}. $$

Here we omit $x-z_{{j^{*}}}$ in the product, where ${j^{*}}\neq j$ is such that $z_{{j^{*}}}=-\overline{z_{j}}$ . We note that $c_{ik}\big(Q_{*}(x)F(x)\overline{F}(-x)\big)^{(k)}(z_{i})=0$ for all $i,k$ except $k=r$ and $i=j$ or $i={j^{*}}$ . It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\Phi\big(Q_{*}(x)F(x)\overline{F}(-x)\big)=c_{jr}\big(Q_{*}(x)F(x)\overline{F}(-x)\big)^{(r)}(z_{j})+c_{{j^{*}}r}\big(Q_{*}(x)F(x)\overline{F}(-x)\big)^{(r)}(z_{{j^{*}}}) \displaystyle\hphantom{\Phi\big(Q_*(x)F(x)\lx@text@overline{F}(-x)\big)}{}=c_{jr}Q_{*}(z_{j})F^{(r)}(z_{j})\overline{F}(-z_{j})+(-1)^{r}c_{{j^{*}}r}Q_{*}(z_{{j^{*}}})F(z_{{j^{*}}})\overline{F}^{(r)}(-z_{{j^{*}}}) \displaystyle\hphantom{\Phi\big(Q_*(x)F(x)\lx@text@overline{F}(-x)\big)}{}=c_{jr}a+c_{{j^{*}}r}\overline{a}, $$

where $a:=Q_{*}(z_{j})F^{(r)}(z_{j})\overline{F}(-z_{j})$ . Pick $a\in\mathbb{C}$ so that

$$ c_{jr}a+c_{{j^{*}}r}\overline{a}=2{\rm Re}(c_{jr}a)<0, $$

and choose $G\in\mathbb{C}[x]$ which gives this value of $a$ (e.g., we can choose $G$ to be linear). Then $\Phi\big(Q_{*}(x)F(x)\overline{F}(-x)\big)<0$ , as desired. ∎

If $\mathcal{A}_{P_{\circ}}$ is the quantization with parameter $P_{\circ}$ then there is a conjugation $\rho_{\circ}$ on $\mathcal{A}_{P_{\circ}}$ given by the formulas

$$ \rho_{\circ}(v)=\lambda_{\circ}u,\qquad\rho_{\circ}(u)=(-1)^{n}\lambda_{\circ}^{-1}v,\qquad\rho_{\circ}(z)=-z, $$

where $\lambda_{\circ}:=(-1)^{\frac{n-n_{\circ}}{2}}\lambda$ . Therefore we can consider the cone of positive definite forms for $\mathcal{A}_{P_{\circ}}$ with respect to $\rho_{\circ}$ .

#### Corollary 4.19.

The cone of positive definite forms on $\mathcal{A}_{P}$ with respect to $\rho$ coincides with the cone of positive definite forms on $\mathcal{A}_{P_{\circ}}$ with respect to $\rho_{\circ}$ . Namely, a trace $T\colon\mathbb{C}[x]\to\mathbb{C}$ for $\mathcal{A}$ gives a positive definite form if and only if $T$ is a trace for $\mathcal{A}_{P_{\circ}}$ that gives a positive definite form on $\mathcal{A}_{P_{\circ}}$ .

#### Proof.

We deduce from Proposition 4.17 that each trace $T$ that gives a positive definite form should have $\Phi=0$ . By Proposition 3.11, in this case $T$ is a trace for the polynomial $P_{\circ}(x)$ . So there exists polynomial $Q_{*}$ such that for $R=R_{1}Q_{*}+R_{0}$ , $\deg R_{0}<\deg Q_{*}$ , and

$$ T(R(z))=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}Q_{*}(x)R_{1}(x)w(x)|{\rm d}x|+\phi(R_{0}). $$

Using Proposition 4.14 and its proof, we deduce that $w$ has no poles and that $w(x)$ and $\lambda w\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)P(x)$ are nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . Therefore

$$ T(R(z))=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}R(x)w(x)|{\rm d}x|+\psi(R_{0}), $$

where $\psi$ is some linear functional. Using Proposition 4.15, we deduce that this trace is positive if and only if $\psi(R_{0})=\sum_{j}c_{j}R_{0}(z_{j})$ , where $c_{j}\geq 0$ and $z_{j}\in{\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ .

Since $(-1)^{\frac{n-n_{\circ}}{2}}\frac{P(x)}{P_{\circ}(x)}$ is positive on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ , we see that $\lambda w\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)P(x)$ is nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $\lambda_{\circ}w\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)P_{\circ}(x)$ is nonnegative on ${\rm i}\mathbb{R}$ . Using Theorem 4.16 we then deduce that $T$ is positive for $P(x)$ if and only if it is positive for $P_{\circ}(x)$ . ∎

So we have proved the following theorem.

#### Theorem 4.20.

Let $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{P}$ be a filtered quantization of $A$ with parameter $P$ equipped with a conjugation $\rho$ such that $\rho^{2}=g_{t}$ . Let $\ell$ be the number of roots $\alpha$ of $P$ such that $|\operatorname{Re}\alpha|<\frac{1}{2}$ counted with multiplicities and $r$ be the number of distinct roots $\alpha$ of $P$ with $\operatorname{Re}\alpha=-\frac{1}{2}$ . Then the cone $\mathcal{C}_{+}$ of $\rho$ -equivariant positive definite traces on $\mathcal{A}$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{C}_{+}^{1}\times\mathcal{C}_{+}^{2}$ , where $\mathcal{C}_{+}^{2}=\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{r}$ , and $\mathcal{C}_{+}^{1}$ is the cone of nonzero polynomials $G$ such that

- $(1)$ $G$ has degree less than $\ell$ ;

- $(2)$ $G(0)=0$ if $t=1$ ;

- $(3)$ $G(X)\geq 0$ when $X>0$ ;

- $(4)$ $G(X)$ is either nonnegative or nonpositive when $X<0$ depending on whether $\rho=\rho_{+}$ or $\rho_{-}$ .

The conditions are the same as in Theorem 4.6.

## 5 Explicit computation of the coefficients $\boldsymbol{a_{k}}$ , $\boldsymbol{b_{k}}$ of the 3-term recurrence for orthogonal polynomials and discrete Painlevé systems

As noted in Section 3.2, to compute the short star-product associated to a trace $T$ , one needs to compute the coefficients $a_{k}$ , $b_{k}$ of the 3-term recurrence for the corresponding orthogonal polynomials:

$$ p_{k+1}(x)=(x-b_{k})p_{k}(x)-a_{k}p_{k-1}(x). $$

Also recall [14] that $a_{k}=\frac{\nu_{k}}{\nu_{k-1}}$ , where $\nu_{k}:=(P_{k},P_{k})$ . Finally, recall that $\nu_{k}=\frac{D_{k}}{D_{k-1}}$ , where $D_{k}$ is the Gram determinant for $1,x,\dots,x^{k-1}$ , i.e.,

$$ D_{k}=\det_{0\leq i,\,j\leq k-1}\big(x^{i},x^{j}\big)=\det_{0\leq i,\,j\leq k-1}(M_{i+j}), $$

where $M_{r}$ is the $r$ -th moment of the weight function $w(x)$ , i.e.,

$$ M_{r}=\int_{{\rm i}\mathbb{R}}x^{r}w(x)|{\rm d}x|. $$

In the even case $w(-x)=w(x)$ we have $b_{k}=0$ , so

$$ p_{k+1}(x)=xp_{k}(x)-a_{k}p_{k-1}(x), $$

and $p_{k}$ can be easily computed recursively from the sequence $a_{k}$ . If the polynomials $p_{k}$ are $q$ -hypergeometric (i.e., obtained by a limiting procedure from Askey–Wilson polynomials), then $D_{k}$ , $\nu_{k}$ , $a_{k}$ admit explicit product formulas, but in general they do not admit any closed expression and do not enjoy any nice algebraic properties beyond the above.

In our case, the hypergeometric case only arises for $n=1$ or, in special cases, $n=2$ , but the fact that the weight function for general $n$ is essentially a higher complexity version of the weight function for $n=1$ suggests that there is still a weaker algebraic structure in the picture.

In fact, by [12] it follows immediately from the fact that the formal Stieltjes transform satisfies an inhomogeneous first-order difference equation with rational coefficients that the corresponding orthogonal polynomials $p_{m}(x)$ in the $x$ -variable satisfy a family of difference equations

$$ \begin{pmatrix}p_{m}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
p_{m-1}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}=A_{m}(x)\begin{pmatrix}p_{m}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
p_{m-1}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix} $$

such that the matrix $A_{m}(x)$ has rational function coefficients of degree bounded by a linear function of $n$ alone. (Here we work with the “ $x$ ” version of the polynomials, to avoid unnecessary appearances of ${\rm i}$ .)

Since the results of [12] are stated in significantly more generality than we need, we sketch how they apply in our special case. Let $Y_{0}$ be the matrix

$$ Y_{0}(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&F(x)\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $F$ is the formal Stieltjes transform of the given trace. Moreover, for each $n$ , let $\frac{q_{n}(x)}{p_{n}(x)}$ be the $n$ -th Padé approximant to $F(x)$ (with monic denominator), so that $\frac{q_{n}(x)}{p_{n}(x)}-F(x)=O\big(x^{-2n-1}\big)$ . If we define

$$ Y_{n}(x):=\begin{pmatrix}p_{n}(x)&-q_{n}(x)\\
p_{n-1}(x)&-q_{n-1}(x)\end{pmatrix}Y_{0}(x) $$

for $n>0$ , then

$$ Y_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}x^{n}+o\big(x^{n}\big)&O\big(x^{-n-1}\big)\\
x^{n-1}+o\big(x^{n-1}\big)&O\big(x^{-n}\big)\end{pmatrix}. $$

#### Lemma 5.1.

The denominator $p_{n}$ of the $n$ -th Padé approximant to $F(x)$ is the degree $n$ monic orthogonal polynomial for the associated linear functional $T$ .

#### Proof.

If $F=F_{T}$ , then we find

$$ p_{n}(x)F(x)=T\bigg(\frac{p_{n}(x)}{x-z}\bigg)=T\bigg(\frac{p_{n}(x)-p_{n}(z)}{x-z}\bigg)+T\bigg(\frac{p_{n}(z)}{x-z}\bigg) $$

(where we evaluate $T$ on functions of $z$ , and $x$ is a parameter). The two terms correspond to the splitting of $p_{n}(x)F(x)$ into its polynomial part and its part vanishing at $x=\infty$ , so that

$$ q_{n}(x)=T\bigg(\frac{p_{n}(x)-p_{n}(z)}{x-z}\bigg) $$

and

$$ T\bigg(\frac{p_{n}(z)}{x-z}\bigg)=p_{n}(x)F(x)-q_{n}(x)=O\big(x^{-n-1}\big). $$

Comparing coefficients of $x^{-m-1}$ for $0\leq m<n$ implies that $T(z^{m}p_{n}(z))=0$ as required. ∎

#### Remark 5.2.

- 1. It also follows that

$$ Y_{n}(x)_{12}=N_{n}x^{-n-1}+O\big(x^{-n-2}\big),\qquad Y_{n}(x)_{22}=N_{n-1}x^{-n}+O\big(x^{-n-1}\big). $$

- 2. Note that this is an algebraic/asymptotic version of the explicit solution of [3] to the Riemann–Hilbert problem for orthogonal polynomials introduced in [7].

#### Lemma 5.3.

We have $\det(Y_{n})=N_{n-1}$ for all $n>0$ .

#### Proof.

The definition of $Y_{n}$ implies that $\det(Y_{n})\in\mathbb{C}[x]$ , while the (formal) asymptotic behavior implies that $\det(Y_{n})=N_{n-1}+O\big(\frac{1}{x}\big)$ . ∎

The inhomogeneous difference equation satisfied by $F$ trivially induces an inhomogeneous difference equation satisfied by $Y_{0}$ :

$$ Y_{0}\big(x+\tfrac{1}{2}\big)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t^{-1}\frac{L(x)}{P(x)}\\[4.30554pt]
0&t^{-1}\end{pmatrix}Y_{0}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&t\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ L(x)=P(x)\big(F\big(x+\tfrac{1}{2}\big)-tF\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\big)\in\mathbb{C}[x]. $$

It follows immediately that $Y_{n}$ satisfies an analogous equation

$$ Y_{n}\big(x+\tfrac{1}{2}\big)=A_{n}(x)Y_{n}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&t\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ A_{n}(x)=\begin{pmatrix}p_{n}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)&-q_{n}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
p_{n-1}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)&-q_{n-1}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&t^{-1}\frac{L(x)}{P(x)}\\[4.30554pt]
0&t^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p_{n}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)&-q_{n}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
p_{n-1}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)&-q_{n-1}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}^{-1}. $$

Since $\det(Y_{n})=N_{n-1}$ , $\det(Y_{0})=1$ , we can use the standard formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix to rewrite this as

$$ A_{n}(x)=N_{n-1}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}p_{n}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)&-q_{n}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
p_{n-1}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)&-q_{n-1}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&t^{-1}\frac{L(x)}{P(x)}\\[4.30554pt]
0&t^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-q_{n-1}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)&q_{n}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
-p_{n-1}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)&p_{n}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}. $$

It follows immediately that $P(x)A_{n}(x)$ has polynomial coefficients. We can also compute the asymptotic behavior of $A_{n}(x)$ using the expression

$$ A_{n}(x)=Y_{n}\big(x+\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&t^{-1}\end{pmatrix}Y_{n}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)^{-1} $$

to conclude that

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{11}=1+\tfrac{n}{x}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big),\qquad \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{12}=-\tfrac{(1-t^{-1})a_{n}}{x}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big), \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{21}=\tfrac{1-t^{-1}}{x}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big),\qquad \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{22}=t^{-1}(1-\tfrac{n}{x})+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big), $$

which when $t=1$ refines to

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{11}=1+\tfrac{n}{x}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big),\qquad \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{12}=-\tfrac{(2n+1)a_{n}}{x^{2}}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{3}}\big), \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{21}=\tfrac{2n-1}{x^{2}}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{3}}\big),\qquad \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{22}=1-\tfrac{n}{x}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big). $$

Restricting to the first column of $Y_{n}(x)$ gives the following.

#### Proposition 5.4.

The orthogonal polynomials satisfy the difference equation

$$ \begin{pmatrix}p_{n}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
p_{n-1}\big(x+\frac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}=A_{n}(x)\begin{pmatrix}p_{n}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
p_{n-1}\big(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}. $$

Note that it is not the mere existence of a difference equation with rational coefficients that is significant (indeed, any pair of polynomials satisfies such an equation!), rather it is the fact that (a) the poles are bounded independently of $n$ , and (b) so is the asymptotic behavior at infinity.

If we consider (for $t\neq 1$ ) the family of matrices satisfying the above conditions; that is, $PA_{n}$ is polynomial, $\det(A_{n})=t^{-1}$ , and

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{11}=1+\tfrac{n}{x}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big),\qquad A_{n}(x)_{12}=O\big(\tfrac{1}{x}\big), \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{21}=\tfrac{1-t^{-1}}{x}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big),\qquad A_{n}(x)_{22}=t^{-1}\big(1-\tfrac{n}{x}\big)+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big), $$

we find that the family is classified by a rational moduli space. To be precise, let $f(x):=$ $\big(1-t^{-1}\big)^{-1}P(x)A_{n}(x)_{21}$ , and let $g(x)\in\mathbb{C}[x]/(f(x))$ be the reduction of $P(x)A_{n}(x)_{11}$ modulo $f(x)$ . Then $f$ and $g$ both vary over affine spaces of dimension $\deg(q)-1$ , and generically determine $A_{n}$ . Indeed, $A_{n}(x)_{21}$ is clearly determined by $f$ , and since $A_{n}(x)_{11}P(x)$ is specified by the asymptotics up to an additive polynomial of degree $\deg(P)-2$ , it is determined by $f$ and $g$ . For generic $f$ , $g$ , this also determines $A_{n}(x)_{22}$ , since the determinant condition implies that for any root $\alpha$ of $f$ , $A_{n}(\alpha)_{11}A_{n}(\alpha)_{22}=t^{-1}$ . Moreover, this constraint forces $P(x)^{2}\big(A_{n}(x)_{11}A_{n}(x)_{22}-t^{-1}\big)$ to be a multiple of $f(x)$ , and thus the unique value of $A_{n}(x)_{12}$ compatible with the determinant condition gives a matrix satisfying the desired conditions.

Moreover, given such a matrix, the three-term recurrence for orthogonal polynomials tells us that the corresponding $A_{n+1}$ is the unique matrix satisfying its asymptotic conditions and having the form

$$ A_{n+1}(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x+\frac{1}{2}-b_{n}&-a_{n}\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}A_{n}(x)\begin{pmatrix}x-\frac{1}{2}-b_{n}&-a_{n}\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}^{-1}. $$

It is straightforward to see that $a_{n}$ , $b_{n}$ are determined by the leading terms in the asymptotics of $A_{n}(x)_{12}$ , and thus in particular are rational functions of the parameters. We thus find that the map from the space of matrices $A_{n}$ to the space of matrices $A_{n+1}$ is a rational map, and by considering the inverse process, is in fact birational, corresponding to a sequence $F_{n}$ of birational automorphisms of $\mathbb{A}^{2\deg(P)-2}$ . Note that the equation $A_{0}$ , though not of the standard form, is still enough to determine $A_{1}$ , and thus gives (rationally) a $\mathbb{P}^{\deg(P)-1}$ worth of initial conditions corresponding to orthogonal polynomials. (There is a $\deg(P)$ -dimensional space of valid functions $F$ , but rescaling $F$ merely rescales the trace, and thus does not affect the orthogonal polynomials.)

#### Example 5.5.

As an example, consider the case $P(x)=x^{2}$ , corresponding, e.g., to

$$ {\rm w}(y)=\frac{{\rm e}^{2\pi cy}}{\cosh^{2}\pi y}, $$

with $c\in(0,1)$ . In this case, $\deg(P)=2$ , so we get a $2$ -dimensional family of linear equations, and thus a second-order nonlinear recurrence, with a 1-parameter family of initial conditions corresponding to orthogonal polynomials. Since the monic polynomial $f$ is linear, we may use its root as one parameter $f_{n}$ , and $g_{n}=A_{n}(f_{n})_{11}$ as the other parameter. We thus find that

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}(x)=\begin{pmatrix}\big(1-\frac{f_{n}}{x}\big)\big(1+\frac{f_{n}+n}{x}\big)+\frac{f_{n}^{2}g_{n}}{x^{2}}&-a_{n}\frac{1-t^{-1}}{x}\big(1-\frac{f_{n+1}}{x}\big)\\
\frac{1-t^{-1}}{x}\big(1-\frac{f_{n}}{x}\big)&t^{-1}\big(\big(1-\frac{f_{n}}{x}\big)\big(1+\frac{f_{n}-n}{x}\big)+\frac{f_{n}^{2}}{g_{n}x^{2}}\big)\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle a_{n}=\frac{t}{(t-1)^{2}}\frac{n^{2}g_{n}-f_{n}^{2}(g_{n}-1)^{2}}{g_{n}} $$

and $f_{n}$ , $g_{n}$ are determined from the recurrence

$$ \displaystyle f_{n+1}=\frac{f_{n}(f_{n}(g_{n}-1)-ng_{n})(f_{n}(g_{n}-1)-n)}{n^{2}g_{n}-f_{n}^{2}(g_{n}-1)^{2}}, \displaystyle g_{n+1}=\frac{(f_{n}(g_{n}-1)-ng_{n})^{2}}{tg_{n}(f_{n}(g_{n}-1)-n)^{2}}. $$

The three-term recurrence for the orthogonal polynomials is then

$$ p_{n+1}(x)=(x-b_{n})p_{n}(x)-a_{n}p_{n-1}(x), $$

where $a_{n}$ is as above and

$$ b_{n}=-f_{n+1}-\frac{(t+1)\big(n+\frac{1}{2}\big)}{t-1}. $$

The initial condition is given by

$$ f_{0}=b_{0}+\frac{t+1}{2(t-1)},\qquad g_{0}=1. $$

(Note that the resulting $A_{0}$ is not actually correct, but this induces the correct values for $f_{1}$ , $g_{1}$ , noting that the recurrence simplifies for $n=0$ to $f_{1}=-f_{0}$ , $g_{1}=1/tg_{0}$ .) It follows from the general theory of isomonodromy deformations [13] that this recurrence is a discrete Painlevé equation (This will also be shown by direct computation in forthcoming work by N. Witte.). We also note that the recurrence satisfies a sort of time-reversal symmetry: there is a natural isomorphism between the space of equations for $t$ , $n$ and the space for $t^{-1}$ , $-n$ , coming (up to a diagonal change of basis) from the duality $A\mapsto\big(A^{\rm T}\big)^{-1}$ , and this symmetry preserves the recurrence. (This follows from the fact that if two equations are related by the three-term recurrence, then so are their duals, albeit in the other order.)

#### Remark 5.6.

The fact that $A_{n}(x)_{12}$ has a nice expression in terms of $a_{n}$ and $f_{n+1}$ follows more generally from the fact (via the three-term recurrence) that

$$ A_{n}(x)_{12}=-a_{n}A_{n+1}(x)_{21}. $$

One similarly has

$$ A_{n}(x)_{22}=A_{n+1}(x)_{11}-\big(x+\tfrac{1}{2}-b_{n}\big)A_{n+1}(x)_{21}, $$

so that in general $f_{n+1}(x)\propto P(x)A_{n}(x)_{12}$ and $g_{n+1}(x)=P(x)A_{n}(x)_{22}\bmod f_{n+1}(x)$ . In particular, applying this to $n=0$ tells us that the orthogonal polynomial case corresponds to the initial condition $f_{1}(x)\propto L(x)$ , $g_{1}(x)=t^{-1}P(x)\bmod L(x)$ .

The above construction fails for $t=1$ , because the constraint on the asymptotics of the off-diagonal coefficients of $A_{n}$ is stricter in that case:

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{21}=\tfrac{2n-1}{x^{2}}+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{3}}\big), \displaystyle A_{n}(x)_{12}=O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{2}}\big). $$

The moduli space is still rational, although the arguments is somewhat subtler. We can still parametrize it by $f_{n}(x):=P(x)A_{n}(x)_{12}$ and $g_{n}(x):=P(x)A_{n}(x)_{11}\bmod f_{n}(x)$ as above, which is certainly enough to determine $P(x)A_{n}(x)_{22}$ modulo $f_{n}(x)$ . This still leaves two degrees of freedom in the diagonal coefficients, but $\det(A_{n}(x))+O\big(\tfrac{1}{x^{4}}\big)$ depends only on the diagonal coefficients and is linear in the remaining degrees of freedom, so we can solve for those. Once again, having determined the coefficients on and below the diagonal, the $21$ coefficient follows from the determinant, and can be seen to have the correct poles and asymptotics. Note that now the dimension of the moduli space is $2\deg(q)-4$ ; that the dimension is even in both cases follows from the existence of a canonical symplectic structure on such moduli spaces, see [13].

There is a similar reduction in the number of parameters when the trace is even (forcing $t=(-1)^{n}$ and $P(x)=(-1)^{n}P(-x)$ ). The key observation in that case is that

$$ Y_{n}(-x)=(-1)^{n}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix}Y_{n}(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix} $$

implying that $A_{n}$ satisfies the symmetry

$$ A_{n}(-x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix}A_{n}(x)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $A_{n}$ is $2\times 2$ and has determinant $t^{-1}=(-1)^{n}$ , this actually imposes linear constraints on the coefficients of $A_{n}$ :

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}(-x)_{11}=(-1)^{n}A_{n}(x)_{22},\qquad \displaystyle A_{n}(-x)_{12}=(-1)^{n}A_{n}(x)_{12}, \displaystyle A_{n}(-x)_{21}=(-1)^{n}A_{n}(x)_{21},\qquad \displaystyle A_{n}(-x)_{22}=(-1)^{n}A_{n}(x)_{11}. $$

In particular, $A_{n}(x)_{21}$ has only about half the degrees of freedom one would otherwise expect, and for any root of that polynomial, $A_{n}(\alpha)_{11}A_{n}(-\alpha)_{11}=1$ , again halving the degrees of freedom (and preserving rationality).

#### Example 5.7.

Consider the case $P(x)=x^{3}+\beta^{2}x$ with $t=-1$ and even trace $\big($ e.g., for $\beta=0$ , the weight function ${\rm w}(y)=\frac{1}{\cosh^{3}\pi y}\big)$ . Then $A_{n}(x)_{21}$ has the form $\frac{2(x^{2}-f_{n})}{x^{3}+\beta^{2}x}$ , and $A_{n}\big(\sqrt{f_{n}}\big)_{11}$ is of norm 1, which can be parametrized in the form

$$ A_{n}\big(\sqrt{f_{n}}\big)_{11}=\frac{g_{n}+\sqrt{f_{n}}}{g_{n}-\sqrt{f_{n}}}. $$

Applying this to both square roots gives two linear conditions on $A_{n}(x)_{11}$ , which suffices to determine it, with $A_{n}(x)_{22}$ following by symmetry and $A_{n}(x)_{12}$ from the remaining determinant conditions. We thus obtain

$$ A_{n}(x)=\begin{pmatrix}\displaystyle 1\!+\!\frac{n(x^{2}\!-\!f_{n})}{x(x^{2}\!+\!\beta^{2})}\!+\!\frac{2f_{n}(f_{n}\!+\!\beta^{2})(g_{n}\!+\!x)}{(g_{n}^{2}\!-\!f_{n})x(x^{2}\!+\!\beta^{2})}&\displaystyle-2a_{n}\frac{x^{2}-f_{n+1}}{x(x^{2}+\beta^{2})}\\[8.61108pt]
\displaystyle 2\frac{x^{2}-f_{n}}{x(x^{2}+\beta^{2})}&\displaystyle\!-\!1\!+\!\frac{n(x^{2}\!-\!f_{n})}{x(x^{2}\!+\!\beta^{2})}\!+\!\frac{2f_{n}(f_{n}\!+\!\beta^{2})(g_{n}\!-\!x)}{(g_{n}^{2}\!-\!f_{n})x(x^{2}\!+\!\beta^{2})}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ a_{n}=-\frac{n^{2}}{4}+\frac{f_{n}(f_{n}+\beta^{2})}{g_{n}^{2}-f_{n}} $$

and $f_{n}$ , $g_{n}$ are determined by the recurrence

$$ \displaystyle g_{n+1}=-\frac{n}{2}-\frac{2g_{n}a_{n}}{ng_{n}-2f_{n}}, \displaystyle f_{n+1}=-\frac{(ng_{n}-2f_{n})^{2}g_{n+1}^{2}}{4f_{n}a_{n}}, $$

with initial condition $f_{1}=-\beta^{2}-\frac{1}{4}-a_{1}$ , $g_{1}=0$ .

#### Remark 5.8.

One can perform a similar calculation for the case $P(x)=x^{4}-e_{1}x^{2}+e_{2}$ with even trace; again, one obtains a second-order nonlinear recurrence, but the result is significantly more complicated, even for $e_{1}=e_{2}=0$ .

In each case, when the moduli space is $0$ -dimensional, so that the conditions uniquely determine the equation, we get an explicit formula for $A_{n}$ . This, of course, is precisely the case that the orthogonal polynomial is classical.
